slides.title: Say please when you ask
slides.text: Please is a kind word. Say it when you ask for a cookie or a turn.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want a cookie. What's a polite way to ask?

options.label: Say "please" when you ask
options.outcome: Exactly right! Please is a kind word to say when you ask for a cookie or a turn.

options.label: Just grab it without asking
options.outcome: Grabbing without asking isn't polite — saying please when you ask is the kind way.

options.label: Demand it loudly
options.outcome: Demanding loudly isn't polite — saying please shows kindness instead.

slides.title: Say thank you
slides.text: Thank you is a kind way to show you noticed someone's help or gift. If someone hands you your dropped crayon, you can smile and say, "Thank you!"

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend gives you a small gift. What's the polite response?

options.label: Say thank you
options.outcome: Exactly right! Thank you is a kind way to show you noticed someone's gift.

options.label: Say nothing
options.outcome: Saying nothing can seem ungrateful — thank you shows you noticed their kindness.

options.label: Complain that it's not what you wanted
options.outcome: Complaining about a gift can hurt the giver's feelings — a simple thank you is much kinder.

slides.title: Say excuse me
slides.text: Excuse me is what you say to get past someone. You say it before you walk by your sister.

widgetConfig.scenario: You need to walk past someone in a narrow hallway. What's the polite thing to say?

options.label: "Excuse me"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Saying excuse me is a polite way to pass by someone.

options.label: Push past without saying anything
options.outcome: Saying excuse me first is much more polite than just pushing past.

options.label: Yell at them to move
options.outcome: A polite 'excuse me' works much better than yelling.

slides.title: Say you are sorry
slides.text: If you hurt someone or cause a problem, saying sorry is one way to show you care. You can also help fix it, like rebuilding blocks you knocked over.

widgetConfig.scenario: You accidentally knock over your friend's blocks. What should you do?

options.label: Say sorry and help rebuild them
options.outcome: Exactly right! Saying sorry and helping fix it, like rebuilding blocks you knocked over, shows you care.

options.label: Walk away and say nothing
options.outcome: Walking away without saying anything doesn't show you care — saying sorry and helping fix it does.

options.label: Blame your friend for building them in your way
options.outcome: Blaming your friend doesn't take responsibility — saying sorry and helping fix it is the better choice.

slides.title: Say hello and goodbye
slides.text: A friendly hello or goodbye can help people feel noticed. You can wave, smile, or say "Hi" in a way that feels comfortable.

widgetConfig.scenario: You arrive at a friend's house. What's a friendly way to greet them?

options.label: Wave, smile, or say "Hi"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A friendly hello like waving or smiling can help people feel noticed.

options.label: Walk in without saying anything
options.outcome: Walking in silently misses a chance to make your friend feel noticed — a friendly hello works better.

options.label: Greetings do not matter
options.outcome: Greetings actually matter — a small hello can make someone feel noticed and welcomed.

slides.title: Wait for your turn
slides.text: Waiting your turn means you let others go first. You wait at the slide until your friend climbs down.

widgetConfig.scenario: You really want to go down the slide, but two other kids are already waiting in line. What should you do?

options.label: Wait patiently in line behind them
options.outcome: That's exactly right! Waiting your turn is fair to everyone, and your turn will come.

options.label: Rush past them to go first
options.outcome: Cutting in line isn't fair to the kids who were waiting first — everyone gets a turn when we wait nicely.

options.label: Complain loudly that it's taking too long
options.outcome: Waiting can feel hard, but a calm wait is kinder than complaining — your turn will come soon!

slides.title: Ask before you take something
slides.text: Always ask before you take someone's toy. Say, 'Can I play with your truck?' and wait to hear yes.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to play with your friend's toy truck. What should you do first?

options.label: Ask "Can I play with your truck?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Always ask before you take someone's toy, and wait to hear yes.

options.label: Just take it without asking
options.outcome: Taking it without asking isn't polite — asking first and waiting for yes is the right way.

options.label: Asking first does not matter
options.outcome: Asking first actually matters a lot — it shows respect for what belongs to someone else.

slides.title: Don't interrupt when someone is talking
slides.text: Try to let someone finish before you speak. If something is urgent, say "Excuse me" and wait for them to notice you.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone is in the middle of talking and you really want to say something. What should you do?

options.label: Wait for them to finish, or say "excuse me" if urgent
options.outcome: Exactly right! Try to let someone finish before you speak, or say excuse me if it's urgent.

options.label: Interrupt right away
options.outcome: Interrupting right away cuts off what they're saying — waiting or saying excuse me is more polite.

options.label: Waiting to talk is never necessary
options.outcome: Waiting for your turn to talk actually matters — it shows you respect what the other person is saying.

slides.title: Use a kind voice
slides.text: A kind voice is calm and respectful. You can still say "no" or disagree without yelling or using hurtful words.

widgetConfig.scenario: You disagree with a friend. What's a kind way to say so?

options.label: Say it calmly, without yelling
options.outcome: Exactly right! A kind voice is calm and respectful — you can still disagree without yelling.

options.label: Yell to make your point
options.outcome: Yelling can hurt feelings and isn't necessary — you can disagree calmly instead.

options.label: You can never disagree politely
options.outcome: You actually can disagree politely — using a calm, kind voice works just fine.

quiz.question: You want a cookie. What should you say?
choices: Can I have a cookie, please?
Give me a cookie now.
quiz.explanation: Please makes an ask sound kind. Saying 'please' shows good manners, like asking nicely for a cookie.

quiz.question: Someone helps you pick up crayons you dropped. What can you say?
choices: Nothing at all.
Thank you!
quiz.explanation: Saying thank you is a kind way to show you noticed someone's help.

quiz.question: You need to walk past your sister. What do you say?
choices: Excuse me.
Move it.
quiz.explanation: Excuse me is a polite way to pass by someone. It is kinder than telling your sister to move.

quiz.question: You knock down your friend's blocks by accident. What should you say?
choices: I'm sorry.
That's your fault.
quiz.explanation: Saying sorry shows you care about your friend's feelings. It helps fix the mistake, like knocking down blocks.

quiz.question: You see your neighbor Mr. Sam outside. What is a friendly thing to do?
choices: Ignore him and keep walking.
Wave and say 'Hi!'
quiz.explanation: A wave and hello let Mr. Sam know you see him. Friendly greetings make people feel noticed.

quiz.question: Your friend is going down the slide first. What should you do?
choices: Wait for your turn.
Push in front of her.
quiz.explanation: Waiting your turn is fair to everyone. Your friend gets to finish the slide before it is your turn.

quiz.question: You want to play with your brother's toy truck. What should you do first?
choices: Grab the truck.
Ask if you can play with it.
quiz.explanation: Asking first shows you respect what belongs to your brother. He gets to say yes before you play with the truck.

quiz.question: Your mom is talking to a friend. What should you do before you speak?
choices: Wait until she stops talking.
Yell over her right away.
quiz.explanation: Waiting your turn to talk is polite. It lets your mom finish her sentence before you say something.

quiz.question: Which voice is the kind way to ask for juice?
choices: A loud, angry voice.
A soft, calm voice.
quiz.explanation: A soft voice sounds friendly and kind. People like to help you more when you ask calmly for juice.

quiz.question: What are 'please' and 'thank you' called?
choices: Polite words that can show respect and appreciation.
Words you only use at school.
quiz.explanation: Please and thank you are common polite words. They do not guarantee a yes, but they can make requests and appreciation sound respectful.

slides.title: Cover your cough or sneeze
slides.text: A cough or sneeze can spread germs. Cover your mouth with your elbow, not your hand.

widgetConfig.scenario: You feel a big sneeze coming on while sitting with friends. What's the polite thing to do?

options.label: Cover your mouth and nose with your elbow or a tissue
options.outcome: Exactly right! Covering a sneeze is polite and helps keep germs from spreading.

options.label: Sneeze openly toward your friends
options.outcome: Sneezing without covering can spread germs — covering it is the polite, healthy choice.

options.label: Hold it in and don't sneeze at all
options.outcome: You can't really hold in a sneeze — covering it with your elbow or a tissue is the polite way to handle it.

slides.title: Use your napkin
slides.text: A napkin wipes your hands and mouth. Use it at dinner instead of your shirt.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your hands get messy at dinner. What should you use to clean them?

options.label: A napkin
options.outcome: Exactly right! A napkin wipes your hands and mouth — use it at dinner instead of your shirt.

options.label: Your shirt
options.outcome: Using your shirt isn't the polite choice — a napkin is what it's there for.

options.label: Nothing, leave them messy
options.outcome: Leaving your hands messy isn't ideal — using a napkin keeps things clean and polite.

slides.title: Chew with your mouth closed
slides.text: Chewing with your mouth closed is polite at the table. No one wants to see your mashed potatoes.

widgetConfig.prompt: Sort each behavior into Polite or Not polite

items.label: Chewing with your mouth wide open
Grabbing or pulling at a pet
Listening when someone is talking to you

slides.title: Wash your hands before you eat
slides.text: Clean hands keep food safe to eat. Wash them with soap before you sit down for dinner.

widgetConfig.scenario: It's almost dinner time. What should you do before you sit down to eat?

options.label: Wash your hands with soap
options.outcome: Exactly right! Washing your hands before eating keeps your food safe and clean.

options.label: Just wipe them on your clothes
options.outcome: Wiping on clothes doesn't clean germs away — washing with soap is what keeps food safe.

options.label: Skip washing since you don't see dirt
options.outcome: Germs can be there even if you can't see them — washing with soap before eating is important.

slides.title: Share your toys
slides.text: Sharing can be kind, but you do not have to give away something special. You can take turns, choose a toy to share, or say, "I'm still using this one."

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend wants to play with your favorite toy. Do you have to give it away completely?

options.label: No — you can take turns or share a different toy
options.outcome: Exactly right! Sharing can be kind, but you do not have to give away something special — taking turns works too.

options.label: Yes, give away anything they ask for
options.outcome: You don't have to give away something special — taking turns or offering a different toy is perfectly fine.

options.label: Never share anything ever
options.outcome: Never sharing anything isn't very kind — taking turns or sharing a different toy works well.

slides.title: Listen when someone is talking to you
slides.text: Listening means giving someone your attention. You can face them, pause what you're doing, or show you're listening in another comfortable way.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone is talking to you. What shows you're listening?

options.label: Facing them and paying attention
options.outcome: Exactly right! Listening means giving someone your attention, like facing them and pausing what you're doing.

options.label: Looking away and ignoring them
options.outcome: Looking away and ignoring them doesn't show you're listening — facing them and paying attention does.

options.label: Listening does not matter
options.outcome: Listening actually matters a lot — it shows someone you care about what they're saying.

slides.title: Say sorry if you bump someone
slides.text: Accidents happen, even soft little bumps. Say sorry right away if you bump into a classmate.

widgetConfig.scenario: You accidentally bump into someone while running at the playground. What should you do?

options.label: Stop and say sorry
options.outcome: That's exactly right! A quick sorry shows you care, even for small accidents.

options.label: Keep running without saying anything
options.outcome: Even a quick accident deserves a sorry — it shows you care about the other person.

options.label: Laugh and keep going
options.outcome: Laughing it off without a sorry can seem like you don't care — a quick sorry is kinder.

slides.title: Ask to leave the table
slides.text: Some families ask children to check before leaving the table. You can say, "I'm finished. May I get up?" and follow your family's routine.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're finished eating and want to get up. What's a polite thing to do?

options.label: Say "I'm finished. May I get up?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Some families ask children to check before leaving the table — asking shows good manners.

options.label: Just get up without saying anything
options.outcome: Getting up without saying anything skips an important step many families expect — asking first is more polite.

options.label: Asking to leave is never necessary
options.outcome: Asking to leave the table actually matters in many families — it's a simple, polite habit.

slides.title: Use gentle hands
slides.text: Gentle hands do not hit, grab, or push. Pet the puppy softly instead of pulling its ears.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're petting a puppy. What should your hands do?

options.label: Pet it softly
options.outcome: Exactly right! Gentle hands do not hit, grab, or push — petting the puppy softly is the kind way.

options.label: Pull its ears
options.outcome: Pulling a puppy's ears can hurt it — gentle hands that pet softly are much kinder.

options.label: Gentleness does not matter with animals
options.outcome: Gentleness actually matters a lot with animals — soft, gentle hands keep them safe and happy.

quiz.question: You feel a sneeze coming. What should you do?
choices: Cover it with your elbow.
Sneeze on your friend.
quiz.explanation: Covering a sneeze with your elbow stops germs from spreading. It keeps your friends from getting sick.

quiz.question: You have sauce on your hands at dinner. What should you use?
choices: Your shirt.
Your napkin.
quiz.explanation: A napkin is made for wiping your hands and mouth. Using your shirt gets food stains on your clothes.

quiz.question: You have food in your mouth. What is polite to do?
choices: Keep your mouth closed while you chew.
Open your mouth so others can see.
quiz.explanation: Chewing with your mouth closed is table manners. No one at dinner wants to see your food.

quiz.question: Before you sit down to eat, what should you do?
choices: Wash your hands.
Go straight to your chair.
quiz.explanation: Washing your hands removes germs before they get on your food. Clean hands help keep you healthy.

quiz.question: Your friend wants a turn with a ball you're using. What is one kind option?
choices: Hide every toy so no one can use anything.
Offer a turn when you're finished or choose something you can share.
quiz.explanation: Sharing can mean taking turns or choosing something you're comfortable sharing. You can also say you're still using a special item.

quiz.question: Your teacher is talking to the class. What should you do?
choices: Keep playing with your toy.
Put the toy down and listen.
quiz.explanation: Listening means giving the speaker your attention. Putting your toy down shows your teacher you are listening.

quiz.question: You bump into a classmate by accident. What should you say?
choices: Nothing, it was an accident.
I'm sorry.
quiz.explanation: Saying sorry shows you care, even for small accidents. It helps your classmate feel better after the bump.

quiz.question: You are done eating dinner. What should you say before you get up?
choices: May I be excused?
I'm done!
quiz.explanation: Asking to be excused is polite before leaving the table. It lets grown-ups know you are finished eating.

quiz.question: You want to pet a puppy. What kind of hands should you use?
choices: Grabby hands.
Gentle hands.
quiz.explanation: Gentle hands do not hurt people or animals. Petting the puppy softly keeps it calm and happy.

quiz.question: What is one reason table manners matter?
choices: They help everyone enjoy the meal together.
They make the food taste different.
quiz.explanation: Manners like a closed mouth and a napkin make mealtime nicer for everyone sitting at the table.

slides.title: Being a polite guest
slides.text: When you visit someone's house, follow their rules even if they are different from yours. Ask before you grab a snack or turn on the TV, since it is not your house.

widgetConfig.prompt: Which of these is NOT polite when visiting someone's house?

items.label: Asking before turning on the TV

widgetConfig.explanation: Grabbing a snack without asking isn't polite when it's not your house — asking first, like the other examples, shows respect.

slides.title: Hold the door for others
slides.text: Holding a door open for the person behind you is a small act of kindness. If your arms are full of grocery bags, someone holding the door really helps a lot.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're walking into a store and someone is right behind you. What's the polite thing to do?

options.label: Hold the door open for them
options.outcome: Exactly right! Holding the door for someone behind you is a simple, kind gesture.

options.label: Let the door close on them
options.outcome: Letting the door close on someone isn't very polite — holding it open is a small kindness.

options.label: Rush through quickly so they have to catch it
options.outcome: Holding the door briefly is more considerate than rushing through and leaving them to catch it.

slides.title: Restaurant manners
slides.text: At a restaurant, use a quiet inside voice and stay seated instead of running between tables. Say 'please' when you order and 'thank you' when the server brings your food.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're at a restaurant. What's polite behavior?

options.label: Use a quiet voice and stay seated
options.outcome: Exactly right! At a restaurant, use a quiet inside voice and stay seated instead of running between tables.

options.label: Run between tables loudly
options.outcome: Running between tables loudly disturbs other diners — staying seated with a quiet voice is much better.

options.label: Restaurant manners do not matter
options.outcome: Restaurant manners actually matter — they help everyone around you enjoy their meal too.

slides.title: Thank you for any gift
slides.text: When someone gives you a gift, thank them for thinking of you, even if the gift is not your favorite. You can be appreciative without pretending you love something you don't.

widgetConfig.scenario: You open a birthday gift and it's not something you were hoping for. What's the polite response?

options.label: Thank them anyway for thinking of you
options.outcome: Exactly right! Saying thank you shows appreciation for their thoughtfulness, no matter the gift itself.

options.label: Say you don't like it
options.outcome: Saying you don't like a gift can hurt the giver's feelings — thanking them for thinking of you is kinder.

options.label: Say nothing and put it aside
options.outcome: Staying silent can seem ungrateful — a simple thank you shows you appreciate the thought.

slides.title: Introduce yourself
slides.text: When you meet someone new, say your name clearly and greet them in a friendly way. Eye contact can be polite in some settings, but a smile, wave, or attentive posture can work too.

widgetConfig.scenario: You meet someone new. What's a good way to introduce yourself?

options.label: Say your name clearly and greet them warmly
options.outcome: Exactly right! Saying your name clearly and greeting someone in a friendly way makes a great first impression.

options.label: Say nothing and walk away
options.outcome: Saying nothing misses a chance to make a good first impression — introducing yourself warmly works much better.

options.label: Introductions do not matter
options.outcome: Introductions actually matter a lot — a clear, friendly one helps start things off well.

slides.title: Take off your shoes if asked
slides.text: House rules are different everywhere. If a family asks guests to remove shoes, follow their rule or politely explain if you need an exception.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend's family asks guests to remove their shoes. What should you do?

options.label: Follow their house rule
options.outcome: Exactly right! House rules are different everywhere — following a family's rule, like removing shoes, shows respect.

options.label: Ignore the request
options.outcome: Ignoring a house rule isn't respectful — following it, or politely explaining if you need an exception, is better.

options.label: House rules never need to be followed
options.outcome: House rules actually do need to be followed as a guest — it's a simple way to show respect.

slides.title: Ask before you touch things at someone's house
slides.text: A friend's house has rules you might not know yet, like which snacks are okay to eat. Ask before you open the fridge, grab a video game, or use someone else's tablet.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're visiting a friend's house and see an interesting toy or item on a shelf. What should you do?

options.label: Ask if it's okay to look at or play with it
options.outcome: Exactly right — asking first shows respect for their home and belongings.

options.label: Pick it up and play with it right away
options.outcome: It's polite to ask first, even if it looks like a toy — it's not your home, so checking first matters.

options.label: Ignore it completely, even if your friend offers
options.outcome: You can enjoy things at a friend's house — just ask first if you're not sure it's okay.

slides.title: Wait to be invited before you help yourself
slides.text: At someone else's house, ask before taking food or using things in the kitchen. A simple "May I have a snack?" is better than guessing what is okay.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're hungry at a friend's house. What's the polite thing to do?

options.label: Ask "May I have a snack?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Asking before taking food or using things in the kitchen is better than guessing what's okay.

options.label: Grab food without asking
options.outcome: Grabbing food without asking isn't polite at someone else's house — asking first is much better.

options.label: Asking first is unnecessary
options.outcome: Asking first actually matters — it respects that it's not your kitchen or your food.

slides.title: Thank the host before you leave
slides.text: Before you head home, find whoever invited you and say thank you for having you over. A quick 'Thanks for having me, I had a lot of fun!' leaves a great last impression.

widgetConfig.scenario: You had fun at a friend's house and it's time to go. What should you do?

options.label: Thank whoever invited you
options.outcome: Exactly right! Before you head home, finding whoever invited you and saying thank you leaves a great last impression.

options.label: Leave without saying anything
options.outcome: Leaving without saying anything misses a chance to leave a great impression — a quick thank you is better.

options.label: Thanking a host does not matter
options.outcome: Thanking a host actually matters a lot — it leaves a great last impression and shows appreciation.

quiz.question: You're visiting a friend's house and want a snack. What should you do?
choices: Ask before you get something from the kitchen.
Open the fridge and help yourself.
quiz.explanation: It is not your house, so the polite move is to ask first. A quick 'Can I have a snack, please?' shows respect for your friend's home.

quiz.question: Your arms are full of grocery bags. What can someone do to help you?
choices: Walk past without noticing.
Hold the door open for you.
quiz.explanation: Holding a door is a small act of kindness that costs nothing but a few seconds. It makes carrying bags through a doorway much easier.

quiz.question: You are eating at a restaurant. What is polite table behavior?
choices: Running between the tables.
Staying seated and using a quiet voice.
quiz.explanation: A restaurant is a shared space where other diners are trying to enjoy their meal too. Staying seated and speaking quietly respects everyone around you.

quiz.question: You get a birthday gift you already own. What should you say?
choices: Thank you, I love it!
Ugh, I already have this.
quiz.explanation: The gift-giver chose it because they were thinking of you, even if it wasn't a perfect match. Saying thank you kindly is what matters, not whether you already own it.

quiz.question: You meet a new kid at camp. What is a good way to introduce yourself?
choices: Say your name and greet them in a friendly way.
Wait for them to guess your name.
quiz.explanation: A clear, friendly introduction helps someone know how to talk with you. Eye contact can be used if comfortable, but it is not the only way to show attention.

quiz.question: You notice a pile of shoes by your friend's front door. What might that mean?
choices: Their family likes collecting shoes.
Shoes come off inside that house.
quiz.explanation: A pile of shoes near the entrance is often a hint that a family takes theirs off indoors. Following their habit shows you're paying attention.

quiz.question: You're at a friend's house and want to play their video game. What should you do first?
choices: Grab the controller and start playing.
Ask if it's okay to play.
quiz.explanation: Someone else's belongings, like a video game console, come with rules you might not know yet. Asking first shows you respect what isn't yours.

quiz.question: You're hungry at a friend's house, but no one has offered a snack yet. What's polite?
choices: Wait to be offered something.
Open the pantry and pick something out.
quiz.explanation: Serving yourself in someone else's kitchen without being asked can feel awkward for the host. Waiting to be offered shows good guest manners.

quiz.question: You're leaving a friend's birthday party. What should you do before you go?
choices: Leave quietly without saying anything.
Thank whoever invited you.
quiz.explanation: A quick 'Thanks for having me, I had fun!' leaves a good last impression on your host. It shows you appreciated being invited.

quiz.question: Why do good guest manners matter?
choices: They make people want to invite you back.
They only matter at fancy events.
quiz.explanation: Being a considerate guest, like asking before touching things or thanking your host, makes people happy to have you over again.

slides.title: Speak politely to adults
slides.text: Use the same basic respect with adults that you use with anyone else: listen, answer clearly, and avoid insulting or dismissive words. Respect does not mean you cannot ask questions or disagree.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teacher asks you a question you don't fully understand. What's the most polite way to respond?

options.label: Sorry, could you explain that a bit more, please?
options.outcome: That's a polite, clear way to ask for help — teachers appreciate respectful questions!

options.label: I don't get it, with a shrug
options.outcome: A flat response without please can come across as rude, even if you don't mean it that way.

options.label: Say nothing and hope it doesn't come up again
options.outcome: Staying silent means you might miss out on understanding — it's polite and totally fine to ask for clarification.

slides.title: Don't shout during a video call
slides.text: A microphone picks up your normal voice just fine, so shouting can hurt everyone's ears. If your family is on a video call, use the same voice you'd use sitting across the table.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're on a video call and want to make sure everyone hears you. Should you shout?

options.label: No — the microphone picks up your normal voice just fine
options.outcome: Exactly right! A microphone picks up your normal voice just fine, so shouting can actually hurt people's ears.

options.label: Yes, always shout on video calls
options.outcome: Shouting isn't necessary — the microphone already picks up your normal speaking voice clearly.

options.label: Shouting helps the microphone work better
options.outcome: Shouting doesn't help the microphone — it just makes the call uncomfortably loud for everyone else.

slides.title: Wait for a pause before you interrupt
slides.text: Jumping into a conversation the second you think of something can make the other person feel unheard. If it's urgent, a quiet 'excuse me' lets you interrupt without seeming rude.

widgetConfig.scenario: You think of something exciting mid-conversation. What should you do?

options.label: Wait for a pause, or say "excuse me" if urgent
options.outcome: Exactly right! Jumping in the second you think of something can make the other person feel unheard — waiting for a pause is more respectful.

options.label: Interrupt immediately
options.outcome: Interrupting immediately can make the other person feel unheard — waiting for a pause works much better.

options.label: Interrupting never bothers anyone
options.outcome: Interrupting can actually bother people a lot — waiting for a pause shows more respect.

slides.title: Keep your elbows off the table
slides.text: Table manners vary by family and culture. A useful rule is to eat neatly, avoid crowding others, and follow the host's lead when you're unsure.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're unsure about table manners at a friend's house. What's a good rule?

options.label: Eat neatly and follow the host's lead
options.outcome: Exactly right! A useful rule is to eat neatly, avoid crowding others, and follow the host's lead when you're unsure.

options.label: Do whatever you want regardless of others
options.outcome: Ignoring others at the table isn't considerate — eating neatly and following the host's lead works better.

options.label: Table manners never matter
options.outcome: Table manners actually matter, especially as a guest — following the host's lead shows respect.

slides.title: Put your phone away at the table
slides.text: If people are eating and talking together, keeping your phone away helps you stay part of the conversation. If you need to check something important, explain briefly first.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're having dinner with family and you get a text message. What's polite?

options.label: Let it wait until after dinner
options.outcome: Exactly! Keeping your phone away during meals shows you value time with the people around you.

options.label: Check it immediately at the table
options.outcome: Checking your phone at the table can feel dismissive to the people you're with — it can usually wait.

options.label: Leave the table to answer it
options.outcome: Letting it wait until after the meal is usually the most polite choice, unless it's truly urgent.

slides.title: Say thank you to a coach, teacher, or bus driver
slides.text: Grown-ups who help you all week, like a coach or bus driver, rarely hear thank you. A simple 'Thanks, Coach!' at the end of practice means more than you'd think.

widgetConfig.scenario: A bus driver helps you every day but rarely hears thanks. What's a kind gesture?

options.label: Say "Thanks!" at the end of the ride
options.outcome: Exactly right! A simple thank you to someone who helps you all week means more than you'd think.

options.label: Never acknowledge them
options.outcome: Never acknowledging their help misses a chance to show appreciation — a quick thanks means a lot.

options.label: Thanking helpers does not matter
options.outcome: Thanking helpers actually matters a lot, even for people who help you every day without much recognition.

slides.title: Knock before entering a room
slides.text: A closed door usually means someone wants privacy, even if it's just your sibling's messy bedroom. Knock and wait for an answer instead of just walking right in unannounced.

widgetConfig.scenario: A door is closed. What should you do before entering?

options.label: Knock and wait for an answer
options.outcome: Exactly right! A closed door usually means someone wants privacy — knocking and waiting respects that.

options.label: Walk right in unannounced
options.outcome: Walking in unannounced can invade someone's privacy — knocking first is much more respectful.

options.label: Closed doors do not mean anything
options.outcome: A closed door usually does mean something — knocking first respects the privacy someone's asking for.

slides.title: Answer the phone politely
slides.text: When answering a family phone, start with a friendly hello. For safety, children do not need to give their full name or personal information to an unknown caller.

widgetConfig.scenario: You answer the family phone. What's polite, and also safe?

options.label: Start with a friendly hello, without sharing personal info to strangers
options.outcome: Exactly right! Starting with a friendly hello is polite, and for safety, you don't need to give personal information to an unknown caller.

options.label: Give your full name and address to anyone who calls
options.outcome: Sharing your full name and address with an unknown caller isn't safe — a friendly hello without personal details is better.

options.label: Answering politely does not matter
options.outcome: Answering politely actually matters — it's a simple, kind way to start any phone call.

slides.title: Wait your turn to talk in a conversation
slides.text: A good conversation is like passing a ball back and forth between two people talking. Let others finish their whole thought before you jump in with your own idea.

widgetConfig.scenario: A good conversation goes back and forth like passing a ball. What should you do?

options.label: Let others finish their whole thought first
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good conversation is like passing a ball back and forth — letting others finish their thought keeps it fair.

options.label: Jump in with your idea before they finish
options.outcome: Jumping in before they finish breaks the back-and-forth feel of a good conversation — waiting is more respectful.

options.label: Taking turns talking does not matter
options.outcome: Taking turns actually matters a lot — it's what makes a conversation feel like a real exchange.

quiz.question: You're talking to your friend's dad. What's a polite way to respond to a question?
choices: Yeah, whatever.
Yes, that sounds good.
quiz.explanation: Simple, clear words like 'yes' instead of 'yeah' sound more respectful to adults. Looking at the person while you answer shows you're paying attention too.

quiz.question: Your family is on a video call with grandma. How loud should you talk?
choices: Shout so the microphone definitely hears you.
Use your normal talking voice.
quiz.explanation: A microphone already picks up a normal voice clearly, so shouting just hurts everyone's ears on the call. Talk the way you would sitting across the table.

quiz.question: You suddenly remember something exciting while your teacher is talking. What should you do?
choices: Wait for a pause, then speak.
Blurt it out right away.
quiz.explanation: Interrupting mid-sentence can make the speaker feel unheard, even if what you have to say is exciting. Waiting for a pause, or saying 'excuse me,' is more polite.

quiz.question: You're eating dinner at a friend's house and aren't sure about their table manners. What's a good approach?
choices: Ignore everyone else's customs.
Eat neatly and follow the host's lead.
quiz.explanation: Table manners differ across families and cultures. Eating neatly and noticing the host's customs is more useful than memorizing one universal rule.

quiz.question: Your phone buzzes during dinner. What's the polite move?
choices: Check it right away.
Leave it in your pocket until the meal ends.
quiz.explanation: Checking your phone at the table tells everyone else that something else matters more than them. Most texts can wait until after the meal.

quiz.question: Your bus driver helps you every single day. When should you thank them?
choices: Never, it's just their job.
Sometimes, with a quick 'thanks!'
quiz.explanation: Grown-ups who help you all week, like a bus driver or coach, rarely hear thank you. A quick 'thanks' means more than you'd expect.

quiz.question: Your sibling's bedroom door is closed. What should you do before going in?
choices: Walk right in.
Knock and wait for an answer.
quiz.explanation: A closed door usually means someone wants privacy, even inside your own house. Knocking first respects that, whether it's your sibling's room or a bathroom.

quiz.question: You answer a family phone and don't recognize the caller. What's a safe, polite start?
choices: Hello. May I ask who's calling?
Give them your full name and address.
quiz.explanation: You can be polite without sharing personal information with an unknown caller.

quiz.question: Your friend keeps talking and talking without letting you say anything. What's missing?
choices: Taking turns in the conversation.
Using a loud voice.
quiz.explanation: A good conversation works like passing a ball back and forth between two people. If one person holds on the whole time, it stops feeling like a real conversation.

quiz.question: Why do small courtesies, like saying thank you to a coach, matter?
choices: They make helpful adults feel appreciated.
They are required by law.
quiz.explanation: A quick thank-you costs nothing but makes the person who helped you, like a coach after practice, feel like their effort was noticed.

slides.title: Texting isn't the same as talking
slides.text: Texting strips away your tone of voice and facial expressions, so a short reply like 'fine' can come across as annoyed even when you didn't mean it that way at all. Adding a few extra words, or a simple emoji, helps the other person read your message the way you actually intended it, instead of guessing at your mood.

widgetConfig.prompt: Which of these texts is most likely to be misread as annoyed?
widgetConfig.explanation: A bare "fine." strips away tone and often reads as annoyed, even when it's not meant that way — adding a few extra words or an emoji helps convey your actual mood.

slides.title: Group chat etiquette
slides.text: A group chat pings on everyone's phone at once, so sending twenty separate one-word messages instead of one combined message can genuinely annoy people trying to focus on homework or dinner. Before you post something off-topic or send a wall of texts, think for a second about whether it's really worth interrupting the whole group right now.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to share ten different short thoughts in a group chat. What's the more considerate way to do it?

options.label: Combine them into fewer, well-organized messages
options.outcome: Exactly! Combining your thoughts into fewer messages is more considerate than pinging everyone's phone twenty times.

options.label: Send all ten as separate one-word messages
options.outcome: Sending many separate pings can be annoying for everyone in the chat — combining them is more considerate.

options.label: It doesn't matter how you send them
options.outcome: It does matter — flooding a group chat with many pings can be inconsiderate to everyone else.

slides.title: Quiet voices in shared spaces
slides.text: Places like libraries, waiting rooms, and movie theaters are shared by people who came expecting some quiet, whether they're studying, waiting nervously, or watching a film. If you need to talk, a hushed voice lets you say what you need without pulling everyone else's attention away from what they're trying to focus on.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're in a library where people are studying. How should you talk?

options.label: In a hushed voice
options.outcome: Exactly right! A hushed voice lets you say what you need without pulling everyone's attention away from what they're focused on.

options.label: As loud as normal
options.outcome: Talking at normal volume in a quiet shared space can disturb people who are studying or focusing — a hushed voice is more considerate.

options.label: Volume does not matter in shared spaces
options.outcome: Volume actually matters a lot in shared quiet spaces like libraries — keeping your voice hushed respects others.

slides.title: Don't block the aisle
slides.text: Standing in the middle of a grocery aisle or a hallway to chat can force other people, including someone pushing a cart or carrying groceries, to awkwardly squeeze past you. Stepping to the side for a moment, especially when you notice someone waiting, keeps the path clear for everyone else trying to get through.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're chatting with a friend in the middle of a grocery aisle. Someone needs to get by. What should you do?

options.label: Step to the side
options.outcome: Exactly right! Stepping to the side for a moment keeps the path clear for everyone else trying to get through.

options.label: Keep blocking the aisle
options.outcome: Blocking the aisle can force someone to awkwardly squeeze past you — stepping aside is much more considerate.

options.label: Blocking an aisle never bothers anyone
options.outcome: Blocking an aisle can actually bother people quite a bit, especially someone pushing a cart or carrying groceries.

slides.title: Respecting personal space
slides.text: Personal space is the amount of room that helps someone feel comfortable. There is no single perfect distance, so notice cues: if someone steps back or looks uncomfortable, give them more room.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're talking to someone and keep stepping closer while they keep stepping back. What's happening?

options.label: You're standing too close, and they need more personal space
options.outcome: Good awareness! Noticing someone stepping back is a clear signal to respect their need for more personal space.

options.label: They're just being unfriendly
options.outcome: Stepping back is usually just about personal space, not unfriendliness — it's polite to notice and respect it.

options.label: Personal space doesn't matter in conversations
options.outcome: Personal space does matter — respecting it helps people feel comfortable during a conversation.

slides.title: Texting at the right time
slides.text: Before sending a non-urgent message very late or very early, think about whether it can wait. People use different notification settings, but considerate timing still matters.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to send a non-urgent text very late at night. What should you consider?

options.label: Whether it can wait until a more considerate time
options.outcome: Exactly right! Before sending a non-urgent message very late or very early, it's worth thinking about whether it can wait.

options.label: Timing never matters for texts
options.outcome: Timing actually matters — considerate timing is worth thinking about, even with different notification settings.

options.label: Always send it immediately no matter the hour
options.outcome: Sending non-urgent texts at any hour without thinking about timing isn't very considerate — waiting can be the better choice.

slides.title: Tone gets lost in text
slides.text: Sarcasm and jokes are easy to read correctly out loud, where your voice and expression do half the work, but they can land as genuinely mean in a flat, silent text message. If a joke might be misread by the person receiving it, it's often safer to say it in person or add something that clearly signals you're joking.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to make a joke in a text message. What's a risk?

options.label: It could be misread as genuinely mean
options.outcome: Exactly right! Sarcasm and jokes are easy to read correctly out loud, but can land as genuinely mean in a flat, silent text.

options.label: Jokes always land perfectly in text
options.outcome: Jokes don't always land perfectly in text — tone is easy to lose, which can make a joke seem mean instead of funny.

options.label: Tone is impossible to misunderstand in texting
options.outcome: Tone is actually very easy to misunderstand in texting, since your voice and expression aren't there to help.

slides.title: Ask before you post a photo of someone
slides.text: A funny or embarrassing photo might feel completely harmless to you, but the person in it might hate how they look in that moment or simply not want it posted online for anyone to see. Asking, 'Is it okay if I post this?' before sharing respects that the photo is about them too, not just about you.

widgetConfig.scenario: You took a funny photo of a friend and want to post it online. What's the polite thing to do first?

options.label: Ask your friend if it's okay to post it
options.outcome: Right call — even a funny, harmless-seeming photo should get a yes from the person in it before you post it.

options.label: Post it right away since it's funny
options.outcome: Even funny photos should get permission first — not everyone wants every photo of themselves posted.

options.label: Post it but tag someone else instead
options.outcome: Mislabeling doesn't solve the real issue — the person in the photo still deserves a say in whether it's posted.

slides.title: Headphone manners in public
slides.text: In shared spaces, use headphones or keep sound low enough that it does not disturb others. Also stay aware of traffic, announcements, and people around you.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're listening to music in a shared space. What's considerate?

options.label: Keep the volume low enough not to disturb others
options.outcome: Exactly right! In shared spaces, keeping sound low enough that it does not disturb others is considerate.

options.label: Play it as loud as you want
options.outcome: Playing it loudly can disturb the people around you — keeping the volume low is more considerate.

options.label: Headphone volume never affects others
options.outcome: Headphone volume can actually affect others nearby — keeping it low is a simple way to be considerate.

quiz.question: You text a one-word reply, 'fine,' to a friend's question. Why might they misread it?
choices: Texting loses tone of voice, so short replies can sound annoyed.
Texting always sounds exactly like talking in person.
quiz.explanation: Without tone of voice or a facial expression, a short word like 'fine' can look flat or annoyed even if you meant it warmly. Adding a few extra words or an emoji usually clears up the confusion for the reader.

quiz.question: You have five quick updates for your group chat. What's more considerate?
choices: Send twenty separate one-word texts.
Combine them into one clear message.
quiz.explanation: A group chat notifies everyone's phone at once, so a flood of separate pings can genuinely annoy people who are busy with homework or dinner. Combining your thoughts into one message respects that everyone else's attention is being interrupted too.

quiz.question: You're in a library and need to ask your friend a question. What should you do?
choices: Talk in your normal loud voice.
Use a hushed, quiet voice.
quiz.explanation: A library is a shared space where other people came expecting quiet, whether they're studying or reading. Lowering your voice lets you still communicate without pulling everyone else's focus away from what they're doing.

quiz.question: You're chatting with a friend in the middle of a busy grocery aisle. What's considerate?
choices: Step to the side so others can pass.
Stay put since you were there first.
quiz.explanation: Blocking an aisle forces other shoppers, including someone pushing a heavy cart, to squeeze awkwardly around you. Moving to the side for a moment costs you nothing and keeps the path clear for people trying to get through.

quiz.question: You're talking to a classmate and notice they keep stepping backward. What's likely happening?
choices: You're standing closer than their personal space allows.
They just don't like standing still.
quiz.explanation: People prefer different amounts of personal space. If someone keeps stepping back or looks uncomfortable, give them more room.

quiz.question: It's 11 p.m. and you have exciting but non-urgent news. Should you text a friend right now?
choices: Yes, exciting news can't wait.
It's more considerate to wait until morning.
quiz.explanation: A late-night text can pull someone's attention away at a genuinely bad moment, even if the news feels urgent to you in the moment. Unless it's a true emergency, waiting for a normal hour is the more considerate choice.

quiz.question: You send a sarcastic joke in a text and your friend gets upset. What likely went wrong?
choices: Sarcasm can be misread as mean without tone of voice.
Your friend has no sense of humor at all.
quiz.explanation: Sarcasm relies on tone of voice and expression to land as a joke, and both disappear in a flat text message. Saying it in person, or adding a clear joking cue, helps prevent it from being misread by the reader.

quiz.question: You took a funny photo of a friend at lunch. What should you do before posting it?
choices: Post it right away since it's funny.
Ask your friend if it's okay to post.
quiz.explanation: A photo that feels harmless to you might embarrass the person in it or simply be something they don't want posted online. Asking first respects that the photo involves their image and their choice, not only your opinion of it.

quiz.question: You're on a crowded bus and want to watch a video. What's the polite way to do it?
choices: Play it out loud for everyone to hear.
Use headphones or keep the volume very low.
quiz.explanation: Playing sound out loud in a shared space forces everyone nearby to listen whether they want to or not, even people trying to rest. Headphones let you enjoy your own video without turning it into the whole bus's problem.

quiz.question: What's a common thread connecting good digital and public-space manners?
choices: Thinking about how your action affects the people around you.
Following whichever rule is easiest for you personally.
quiz.explanation: Whether it's a loud video, a blocked aisle, or a late-night text, the same question applies: how does this affect the people nearby right now? Considering that before you act is really the core of good manners.

slides.title: Disagreeing without being disagreeable
slides.text: You can tell a friend you think they're wrong without attacking them personally, by aiming your words at the idea itself instead of at the person holding it. Saying 'I see it differently, here's why' invites a real conversation and keeps things open, while 'that's a dumb idea' just shuts the whole thing down.

widgetConfig.scenario: At dinner, a family member says something you strongly disagree with. What's the most respectful response?

options.label: I see it differently — here's why...
options.outcome: That's a respectful way to disagree — sharing your view calmly keeps the conversation friendly instead of turning into an argument.

options.label: That's a ridiculous thing to say.
options.outcome: Dismissing someone's opinion harshly can shut down the conversation and hurt feelings, even if you have a good point.

options.label: Stay quiet even though it bothers you
options.outcome: You don't have to stay silent — sharing your view respectfully is totally fine, even at the dinner table.

slides.title: Really listen before you respond
slides.text: It's tempting to plan your comeback while the other person is still talking, but that means you're not actually hearing their point or understanding where they're coming from. Waiting until they finish, and maybe repeating back what you heard in your own words, shows you took their side of the disagreement seriously.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend is still talking, but you're already planning what you'll say back. What's the better approach?

options.label: Focus on really listening before responding
options.outcome: Exactly! It's tempting to plan your comeback while someone is still talking, but really listening first leads to a better conversation.

options.label: Keep planning your response instead of listening
options.outcome: Planning your response while they're still talking means you might miss what they're actually saying — listening first is better.

options.label: Interrupt them to say your point first
options.outcome: Interrupting cuts off what they're saying — waiting and really listening first is more respectful and effective.

slides.title: A real apology names what happened
slides.text: 'Sorry you're upset' quietly blames the other person's reaction instead of owning your own part in causing it in the first place. A sincere apology, like 'I'm sorry I read your diary without asking, that wasn't fair to you,' names the specific thing you actually did wrong instead of staying vague.

widgetConfig.scenario: Which is a more sincere apology after reading someone's diary without asking?

options.label: "I'm sorry I read your diary without asking, that wasn't fair to you"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Naming the specific thing you actually did wrong, instead of staying vague, makes a sincere apology.

options.label: "Sorry you're upset"
options.outcome: This quietly blames the other person's reaction instead of owning what you actually did — naming the specific action is more sincere.

options.label: Saying nothing at all
options.outcome: Saying nothing skips the apology entirely — naming what happened is a much more sincere approach.

slides.title: An apology means changing next time
slides.text: Saying sorry for the same thing over and over, without ever changing your behavior afterward, starts to feel hollow and even a little insulting to the person you keep apologizing to. A real apology usually comes paired with some genuine, visible effort to actually do things differently going forward.

widgetConfig.scenario: You keep apologizing for the same thing without ever changing. How does this feel to the other person?

options.label: Hollow, since nothing actually changes
options.outcome: Exactly right! Saying sorry for the same thing over and over without changing starts to feel hollow, even insulting.

options.label: Just as sincere every time
options.outcome: Repeated apologies with no real change tend to feel less sincere each time, not just as sincere.

options.label: Apologies never need real change behind them
options.outcome: A real apology usually comes paired with genuine effort to actually do things differently — change matters.

slides.title: Being a considerate overnight guest
slides.text: A good overnight guest makes their bed or folds up the sleeping bag in the morning, keeps their stuff from spreading through the whole house, and asks before raiding the fridge for a midnight snack. Small habits like these, repeated over one weekend, make a host genuinely glad they invited you.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're staying overnight at a friend's house. What's a considerate thing to do?

options.label: Follow their family's routines and help tidy up after yourself
options.outcome: Exactly right! Respecting their household's way of doing things and helping out shows you're a considerate guest.

options.label: Expect them to do everything exactly like your house
options.outcome: Every household is a little different — adapting to their routines shows respect, rather than expecting things to match your own home.

options.label: Leave your things scattered everywhere
options.outcome: Being tidy and helping clean up shows consideration for your hosts and their home.

slides.title: Every family's rules are a little different
slides.text: One house might let you keep shoes on inside, while another expects everyone to take theirs off the second they walk through the door, and neither family is doing it wrong. Paying attention to what a friend's family actually does, instead of assuming your own house rules apply everywhere you go, shows real respect.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your friend's family has different house rules than yours. What shows respect?

options.label: Paying attention to their rules instead of assuming yours apply
options.outcome: Exactly right! Paying attention to what a friend's family actually does, instead of assuming your own rules apply, shows real respect.

options.label: Assuming your house rules apply everywhere
options.outcome: Assuming your own rules apply everywhere can come across as disrespectful — paying attention to their rules is better.

options.label: House rules are always exactly the same everywhere
options.outcome: House rules actually vary quite a bit between families — paying attention to each one shows respect.

slides.title: Following the host's lead at meals
slides.text: If you're unsure about a meal custom, watch what others do or politely ask. Different families and cultures may start eating, use utensils, or serve food in different ways.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're unsure about a meal custom at someone's house. What should you do?

options.label: Watch what others do or politely ask
options.outcome: Exactly right! If you're unsure about a meal custom, watching what others do or politely asking is the best approach.

options.label: Do whatever you would do at home, regardless
options.outcome: Doing things exactly as you would at home can clash with a different family's customs — watching or asking works better.

options.label: Meal customs are always identical everywhere
options.outcome: Meal customs actually vary a lot between families and cultures — watching or asking helps you follow along respectfully.

slides.title: Handling an awkward moment at someone's house
slides.text: If you accidentally break something or spill a drink at a friend's house, owning up right away — 'I'm sorry, I knocked over the glass, let me help clean it up' — goes a lot further than staying quiet and hoping nobody notices what happened.

widgetConfig.scenario: You accidentally spill a drink at a friend's house. What's the better response?

options.label: Own up right away and offer to help clean it
options.outcome: Exactly right! Owning up right away and offering to help goes a lot further than staying quiet and hoping nobody notices.

options.label: Stay quiet and hope nobody notices
options.outcome: Staying quiet and hoping nobody notices rarely goes well — owning up right away is much better.

options.label: Blame someone else for the spill
options.outcome: Blaming someone else for your own accident isn't honest — owning up right away is the better response.

slides.title: Saying thank you after you stay over
slides.text: A quick text the next day, 'Thanks for letting me stay over, I had a great time,' tells a host their effort planning meals and activities didn't go unnoticed. It takes about ten seconds to send and makes them noticeably more likely to invite you back again.

widgetConfig.scenario: You stayed over at a friend's house. What's a thoughtful thing to do the next day?

options.label: Send a quick thank-you text
options.outcome: Exactly right! A quick thank-you text tells a host their effort didn't go unnoticed, and makes them more likely to invite you back.

options.label: Never mention it again
options.outcome: Never mentioning it again misses a chance to show appreciation — a quick thank-you text means a lot to a host.

options.label: Thank-you texts do not matter to hosts
options.outcome: Thank-you texts actually matter a lot to hosts — they notice when their effort is appreciated.

quiz.question: You disagree with a friend's opinion in a group discussion. What's the more respectful way to say so?
choices: 'That's such a dumb idea.'
'I see it differently — here's why.'
quiz.explanation: Attacking the idea instead of the person keeps the conversation open instead of shutting it down entirely. Saying 'I see it differently, here's why' invites your friend to actually hear and consider your reasoning.

quiz.question: While a friend is explaining why they're upset with you, what should you be doing?
choices: Planning what you'll say back to defend yourself.
Actually listening to their side of it.
quiz.explanation: Planning your comeback while someone is still talking means you miss what they're actually saying and why it matters to them. Listening fully, and repeating back what you heard, shows you're taking their point of view seriously.

quiz.question: Which of these is a more sincere apology?
choices: 'Sorry you're upset.'
'I'm sorry I read your diary, that wasn't fair to you.'
quiz.explanation: 'Sorry you're upset' quietly blames the other person's reaction rather than owning what you actually did. Naming the specific action, like reading a diary without asking, shows you understand exactly why it hurt them.

quiz.question: You've apologized for being late three times this month but keep doing it. What's missing?
choices: Actually changing your behavior, not just the words.
Nothing — apologizing every time is enough.
quiz.explanation: Repeating the same apology without changing anything starts to feel hollow and even insulting to the person hearing it. A real apology usually comes paired with genuine effort to actually do things differently next time.

quiz.question: You're staying overnight at a friend's house. What's a considerate morning habit?
choices: Leave your sleeping bag and stuff scattered around.
Fold up your sleeping bag and tidy your area.
quiz.explanation: Small habits like folding your sleeping bag and keeping your things contained make a host genuinely glad they invited you over. It shows you're thinking about their space, not just your own comfort.

quiz.question: Your friend's family takes their shoes off inside, but yours never does. What should you do at their house?
choices: Take your shoes off like their family does.
Keep your shoes on since that's what you're used to.
quiz.explanation: Every family has slightly different house rules, and a good guest pays attention to what the host's family actually does day to day. Following their habit, even if it differs from your own, shows real respect.

quiz.question: You're at a formal dinner and aren't sure which fork to use. What's a simple way to figure it out?
choices: Watch what your host is doing and match it.
Guess and hope it doesn't matter.
quiz.explanation: Watching your host's lead is a simple, low-pressure way to handle an unfamiliar situation without asking out loud. You don't need to memorize every rule if you're willing to observe and match what's happening around you.

quiz.question: You accidentally spill a drink at a friend's house. What's the best response?
choices: Say nothing and hope no one notices.
Own up right away and offer to help clean it up.
quiz.explanation: Owning the mistake immediately, and offering to help fix it, shows far more respect than hoping it goes unnoticed. Most hosts appreciate honesty and a quick offer to help far more than a hidden mess found later.

quiz.question: You stayed overnight at a friend's house last night. What's a thoughtful thing to do today?
choices: Send a quick thank-you text.
Wait for them to bring it up first.
quiz.explanation: A short text like 'Thanks for having me, I had a great time' takes seconds but tells your host their planning was noticed. It also makes them noticeably more likely to invite you again next time.

quiz.question: What makes an apology feel sincere rather than empty?
choices: Naming what you did wrong and trying to change it.
Saying the word 'sorry' as fast as possible.
quiz.explanation: A sincere apology names the specific thing you did wrong and comes with real effort to behave differently going forward. Just saying the word 'sorry' quickly, without either part, rarely feels genuine to the person hearing it.

slides.title: Ordering politely at a restaurant
slides.text: Talking directly to the server, saying 'please' and 'thank you,' and looking up from your phone while you order all make the interaction feel human instead of purely transactional. Servers deal with dozens of orders every single shift, and a little courtesy from a young customer genuinely stands out to them.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're ordering food at a restaurant. What's the polite way to do it?

options.label: Talk directly to the server, saying "please" and "thank you"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Talking directly to the server, saying please and thank you, and listening to their questions is the polite way to order.

options.label: Point at the menu without saying a word
options.outcome: Pointing silently skips a chance to be polite — speaking directly with please and thank you is better.

options.label: Order through a parent instead of speaking yourself, every single time
options.outcome: Speaking for yourself to the server, when you're able to, is a good way to practice polite, direct communication.

slides.title: Basic tipping awareness
slides.text: In the United States, tipping is common at many sit-down restaurants and some other services. Customs differ by country and situation, so it's useful to ask an adult or check local expectations.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're unsure whether tipping is expected somewhere. What's a smart move?

options.label: Ask an adult or check local expectations
options.outcome: Exactly right! Tipping customs differ by country and situation, so asking an adult or checking local expectations is smart.

options.label: Assume the same rule applies everywhere
options.outcome: Tipping customs actually vary quite a bit by place — assuming one rule applies everywhere can lead to mistakes.

options.label: Tipping customs never vary by place
options.outcome: Tipping customs do vary by place — checking local expectations helps you know what's appropriate.

slides.title: Phones at the table
slides.text: Scrolling through your phone while everyone else at the table is talking sends the message that whatever's on your screen matters more than the conversation happening in front of you. Keeping it face-down or tucked away during a meal, even a quick fast-food one, keeps you actually present with the people you're with.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're at a restaurant with family and everyone's phone is away except yours. What should you do?

options.label: Put your phone away too, to match the group
options.outcome: Good instinct! Matching the group's effort to be present together is a thoughtful, polite choice.

options.label: Keep using yours since no one said anything
options.outcome: Even without being told, noticing the group norm and matching it is a polite, thoughtful choice.

options.label: Tell everyone else to use their phones too
options.outcome: Following the group's more polite choice (putting phones away) fits the moment better than pulling others away from it.

slides.title: Adapting to someone else's house rules
slides.text: A respectful guest notices the host's routines and asks when unsure. You can adapt to different customs while still speaking up about allergies, safety, privacy, or other important needs.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're a guest with a food allergy, but the house has different customs than yours. What should you do?

options.label: Adapt to their customs while still speaking up about your allergy
options.outcome: Exactly right! A respectful guest adapts to different customs while still speaking up about allergies, safety, or other important needs.

options.label: Stay silent about the allergy to avoid being rude
options.outcome: Staying silent about a real allergy isn't safe — you can adapt to customs while still speaking up about important needs.

options.label: Ignore their house customs completely
options.outcome: Ignoring their house customs isn't respectful — adapting to them, while still voicing important needs, is the better balance.

slides.title: Not blocking shared walkways
slides.text: A cluster of friends stopped in the middle of a hallway or a store entrance can force other people into the wall, or even out into the street, just to get around your group. Moving your conversation to the side, out of the main path of foot traffic, takes barely any effort and avoids the problem entirely.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your group of friends is chatting in the middle of a store entrance. What's considerate?

options.label: Move the conversation to the side
options.outcome: Exactly right! Moving your conversation to the side, out of the main path, takes barely any effort and avoids the problem entirely.

options.label: Keep blocking the entrance
options.outcome: Blocking the entrance can force other people to squeeze past or go around your group — moving aside is much more considerate.

options.label: Blocking a walkway never affects anyone
options.outcome: Blocking a walkway can actually affect quite a few people — moving to the side avoids the problem entirely.

slides.title: RSVPing and showing up on time
slides.text: When you're invited somewhere, reply by the requested date if you can. Arriving around the agreed time helps the host plan, and if you're running late, send a quick update.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're invited to an event. What's the polite way to respond?

options.label: Reply by the requested date and arrive on time
options.outcome: Exactly right! Replying by the requested date helps the host plan, and arriving around the agreed time respects their effort.

options.label: Never respond at all
options.outcome: Never responding leaves the host unable to plan properly — replying by the requested date is much more considerate.

options.label: Showing up whenever you want is always fine
options.outcome: Arriving whenever you want can disrupt a host's plans — showing up around the agreed time respects their effort.

slides.title: Disagreeing with an adult, respectfully
slides.text: You can push back on a rule or a decision from a teacher or coach without being rude about it, by asking a genuine question instead of just arguing the point. 'Can you help me understand why?' usually gets further than 'That's not fair,' even if you still end up disagreeing after hearing the answer.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teacher makes a statement you think is incorrect. What's the most respectful way to handle it?

options.label: Politely ask a clarifying question or share your perspective calmly
options.outcome: Good approach — respectfully questioning or sharing your view, rather than staying silent or arguing, keeps the conversation constructive.

options.label: Argue loudly that they're wrong
options.outcome: Arguing loudly can come across as disrespectful, even if your point is valid — a calm, respectful approach works better.

options.label: Stay silent even though you think they're wrong
options.outcome: You don't have to stay silent — respectfully sharing a different perspective is appropriate, even with an adult.

slides.title: A sincere apology, step by step
slides.text: A strong apology usually has three parts: naming exactly what you did, acknowledging how it actually affected the other person, and saying what you'll do differently going forward. 'I'm sorry I left you out, that must have felt lonely, I'll invite you next time' hits all three parts clearly.

widgetConfig.prompt: Tap the three parts of a strong apology in order

quiz.question: You're ordering food at a restaurant while still texting on your phone. What's the more polite approach?
choices: Keep texting while you order without looking up.
Look up and talk directly to the server.
quiz.explanation: Servers handle many orders in a single shift, and looking up to order politely makes the interaction feel human rather than transactional. A little eye contact and a genuine 'please' actually stand out to them.

quiz.question: Your family's restaurant bill is higher than the menu prices added up. What's a likely reason?
choices: The menu prices were printed wrong.
A tip is often expected as part of the total.
quiz.explanation: In many places, a tip is an expected part of how servers are actually paid, not just an optional bonus for great service. That's why the final total at a sit-down restaurant usually runs higher than the listed menu prices alone.

quiz.question: Everyone at the dinner table is talking, but you're scrolling on your phone instead. What message does that send?
choices: That the conversation isn't worth your attention.
Nothing — phones don't affect a conversation.
quiz.explanation: Scrolling while others are talking signals that whatever's on your screen matters more than the people sitting right in front of you. Keeping your phone face-down during a meal helps you actually stay present in the moment.

quiz.question: Your friend's family eats dinner mostly in silence, but yours is loud and chatty. What should you do at their table?
choices: Match their quieter volume instead of your usual one.
Talk at your normal volume since that's what feels natural.
quiz.explanation: Neither style of family dinner is actually wrong, but a considerate guest adjusts to the room they're in rather than expecting the room to adjust to them. Matching their volume shows real awareness of your surroundings.

quiz.question: You and three friends are talking in the middle of a store entrance. What's considerate?
choices: Stay put since you're not blocking that much.
Move to the side, out of the main path.
quiz.explanation: A cluster of people blocking an entrance forces other shoppers to squeeze around your group or step out of the way entirely. Stepping to the side takes almost no effort and clears the path for everyone else.

quiz.question: You get invited to a birthday party. What's the polite way to respond?
choices: Reply with a clear yes or no.
Just show up if you feel like it, or don't.
quiz.explanation: A clear RSVP, even a short text, helps the host plan food, seating, and activities properly ahead of time. Showing up unannounced, or simply not responding at all, makes it much harder for them to prepare.

quiz.question: You disagree with a rule your coach just made. What's a more effective way to push back?
choices: Say 'that's not fair' and walk off.
Ask 'Can you help me understand why?'
quiz.explanation: Asking a genuine question invites the coach to explain their reasoning and treats the disagreement as an actual conversation. It tends to go further than a flat objection, even if you still disagree once you hear the answer.

quiz.question: Which of these apologies covers all three parts of a strong apology?
choices: 'I'm sorry I left you out, that must have felt lonely, I'll invite you next time.'
'Sorry, whatever, let's just move on.'
quiz.explanation: A strong apology names the specific action, acknowledges its real effect on the other person, and says what will change going forward. The first example hits all three parts clearly; the second names and promises nothing.

quiz.question: At a sit-down restaurant in the United States, why might your family add a tip?
choices: Because tipping is a common part of restaurant service in the U.S.
Because every country has exactly the same tipping rules.
quiz.explanation: Tipping is common in many U.S. restaurants, but customs differ by country and type of service.

quiz.question: What connects respectful disagreement with an adult and a sincere apology to a friend?
choices: Both involve actually considering the other person's side.
Both require you to always say the other person is right.
quiz.explanation: Respectful disagreement means genuinely asking why instead of just arguing, and a sincere apology means genuinely naming the impact on the other person. Neither one requires agreeing you're wrong — both require real, honest consideration.

slides.title: First impressions in an interview
slides.text: First impressions come from preparation, punctuality, and a respectful greeting. A handshake or direct eye contact may be common in some settings, but they are not required everywhere; follow the other person's cues.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're about to walk into a job interview. What helps create a good first impression?

options.label: Preparation, punctuality, and a respectful greeting
options.outcome: Exactly! First impressions come from preparation, punctuality, and a respectful greeting.

options.label: Showing up late with no preparation
options.outcome: Showing up late and unprepared tends to hurt a first impression — preparation and punctuality help far more.

options.label: First impressions never matter in an interview
options.outcome: First impressions actually matter a lot in an interview — preparation and punctuality make a real difference.

slides.title: Email tone reads differently than speech
slides.text: A message that would sound perfectly normal out loud can look curt or annoyed in an email, because writing strips away the warmth in your voice. Opening with 'Hi Ms. Patel,' and closing with 'Thanks, Jordan,' instead of diving straight into a request costs two extra lines but changes how the whole message lands.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're emailing a teacher to ask for an extension, and you're tempted to write it exactly like you'd text a friend. What should you do instead?

options.label: Use a more formal, clear tone since email can read more harshly than speech
options.outcome: Good instinct — casual phrasing in email can come across as careless or even rude, since tone is harder to read in writing. A bit more formality helps.

options.label: Send it exactly like a text to a friend
options.outcome: Overly casual phrasing can come across as disrespectful in an email, even if that's not how you meant it — a little more formality helps the message land well.

options.label: Don't send an email, just hope they notice
options.outcome: Not communicating at all leaves your request unaddressed — a clear, appropriately toned email is the better move.

slides.title: Speaking to teachers and other authority figures
slides.text: Use the name or title a teacher, coach, or supervisor asks you to use. A respectful tone and clear request matter more than guessing the 'correct' form of address.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teacher asks to be called by a specific title and name. What should you do?

options.label: Use the name or title they asked for
options.outcome: Exactly right! Use the name or title a teacher, coach, or supervisor asks you to use — it's a simple sign of respect.

options.label: Use whatever nickname you prefer
options.outcome: Using your own preferred nickname instead of what they asked for isn't respectful — using their requested name is better.

options.label: Ignore their preference since it does not matter
options.outcome: Their preference actually does matter — using the name or title they asked for shows respect.
