slides.title: Professional etiquette at a first job
slides.text: Showing up on time, texting ahead if you're going to be even five minutes late, and asking 'Is there anything else I should be doing?' during slow moments all build a reputation as someone reliable. Employers remember reliability, sometimes called dependability, far more than they remember any single impressive thing you did once.

widgetConfig.scenario: You might be five minutes late to your first job. What builds a reputation as reliable?

options.label: Texting ahead to give a heads-up
options.outcome: Exactly right! Texting ahead if you're going to be late builds a reputation as reliable — employers remember this far more than any single impressive moment.

options.label: Saying nothing and showing up whenever
options.outcome: Saying nothing and showing up whenever doesn't build trust — texting ahead shows reliability employers remember.

options.label: Reliability does not matter to employers
options.outcome: Reliability actually matters a huge amount to employers — it's something they remember far more than a single impressive moment.

slides.title: Text tone with adults you don't know well
slides.text: Messages to a teacher, coach, or employer are usually clearer when you use complete sentences and a slightly more formal tone than you might with close friends. Adjusting your communication style to the situation is a normal social skill.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're texting a teacher or employer. What tone works best?

options.label: Complete sentences and a slightly formal tone
options.outcome: Exactly right! Messages to a teacher, coach, or employer are usually clearer with complete sentences and a slightly more formal tone.

options.label: The exact same casual tone as with close friends
options.outcome: Using the exact same casual tone with a teacher or employer as with close friends can come across as too informal.

options.label: Tone never matters in texts to adults
options.outcome: Tone actually matters a lot in texts to adults you don't know well — a slightly more formal tone is usually clearer and more respectful.

slides.title: Handling a scheduling conflict gracefully
slides.text: If you need to cancel or reschedule with a teacher, coach, or employer, saying so as early as possible and offering an alternative — 'Could we meet Thursday instead?' — shows more consideration than a last-minute cancellation ever does. Giving someone advance notice, sometimes called a courtesy heads-up, respects that their time has value too.

widgetConfig.scenario: You need to reschedule with a coach. What shows more consideration?

options.label: Giving early notice and offering an alternative time
options.outcome: Exactly right! Saying so as early as possible and offering an alternative shows far more consideration than a last-minute cancellation.

options.label: Canceling last-minute with no notice
options.outcome: A last-minute cancellation with no notice shows little consideration for the other person's time — early notice is much better.

options.label: Rescheduling never requires any consideration
options.outcome: Rescheduling actually does require consideration — giving early notice respects that someone else's time has value too.

slides.title: Asking for help without feeling embarrassed
slides.text: Asking a teacher or supervisor a clarifying question, 'Could you walk me through that step again?', reads as engaged and conscientious, not as incompetent, to almost everyone who has ever managed or taught someone else. Staying silent and guessing usually creates a bigger problem later than a two-second question would have.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're struggling with a work task and worried asking for help will make you look incapable. What's the better mindset?

options.label: Asking for help, when needed, is seen as responsible, not weak
options.outcome: Exactly — most professionals respect someone who asks for clarification rather than struggling silently and making costly mistakes.

options.label: Avoid asking no matter what, to seem capable
options.outcome: Struggling silently often leads to bigger mistakes — asking for help when genuinely needed is usually seen as responsible, not weak.

options.label: Only ask if you're about to fail completely
options.outcome: Waiting until the last moment makes the situation harder to fix — asking earlier when you're genuinely stuck is the smarter move.

slides.title: Following up with a thank-you note
slides.text: A short thank-you message after an interview, recommendation, or meaningful favor can show appreciation. Keep it sincere and specific rather than treating it like a trick to impress someone.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone gave you a meaningful favor or recommendation. What's a good follow-up?

options.label: A short, sincere thank-you message
options.outcome: Exactly right! A short thank-you message after a meaningful favor shows appreciation — keep it sincere and specific.

options.label: Never mentioning it again
options.outcome: Never mentioning it again misses a chance to show real appreciation — a short, sincere thank-you is a kind follow-up.

options.label: Thank-you notes are just a trick to impress people
options.outcome: A genuine thank-you note isn't a trick — it's a sincere, specific way to show real appreciation.

quiz.question: You arrive a little early for an interview and greet the interviewer respectfully. Why does this matter?
choices: Preparation and courtesy help create a positive first impression.
Interviewers only care about your resume, not behavior.
quiz.explanation: Punctuality, preparation, and a respectful greeting help show that you take the meeting seriously. The exact greeting can vary by person and culture.

quiz.question: You need to ask your teacher for an extension. Which email opening is more effective?
choices: 'hey need more time on the essay'
'Hi Ms. Patel, I wanted to ask about the essay deadline.'
quiz.explanation: Writing strips away the warmth of your actual speaking voice, so a blunt message can read as curt even if you didn't mean it that way. A greeting and a full sentence cost two extra lines but change how the whole request lands.

quiz.question: You want to ask your teacher a quick question after class. What's a respectful way to start?
choices: Just launch into the question mid-hallway.
'Could I ask you something after class?'
quiz.explanation: Framing a request instead of just launching into it signals respect for the teacher's time and attention without being stiff or overly formal. Most teachers notice that small shift, even if they never say so out loud.

quiz.question: At your first part-time job, what habit builds a reputation as reliable over time?
choices: Showing up on time and texting ahead if you'll be late.
Doing one impressive thing and then relaxing.
quiz.explanation: Employers remember dependability — consistent small habits like punctuality — far more than a single standout moment. A quick heads-up text about being five minutes late shows the same reliability as showing up exactly on time.

quiz.question: You text your new boss the same way you text your friends, with no capital letters and lots of emoji. What might happen?
choices: It could come across as careless, even if you mean no disrespect.
Nothing — texting is texting, no matter who it's to.
quiz.explanation: Adjusting your tone to fit the relationship, sometimes called adjusting your communication style, is something most people already do without noticing. A more formal text to a boss than to a friend isn't fake — it matches the relationship.

quiz.question: You can't make your usual shift this week. What's the more considerate way to handle it?
choices: Cancel at the last minute without an explanation.
Give notice early and suggest an alternative time.
quiz.explanation: A courtesy heads-up, given as early as possible, respects that your employer's schedule and time have real value too. Offering an alternative, like 'Could we swap to Thursday?', shows you're still trying to make it work.

quiz.question: You don't fully understand instructions your supervisor gave you. What's the better move?
choices: Guess and hope it works out.
Ask a clarifying question.
quiz.explanation: Asking a clarifying question, like 'Could you walk me through that step again?', reads as engaged, not incompetent, to almost anyone who has managed people. Guessing silently usually creates a bigger problem later than a quick question would have.

quiz.question: You just finished a job interview. What's a small gesture that tends to be remembered?
choices: Sending a short thank-you note afterward.
Not following up at all, since the interview already happened.
quiz.explanation: A short thank-you email takes about two minutes to write but is rare enough that it genuinely sticks in an interviewer's memory. That small extra effort disproportionately shapes how you're remembered compared to everyone who skipped it.

quiz.question: Why might addressing a teacher as 'Ms. Patel' instead of her first name matter, even though it seems small?
choices: It signals respect without needing to be stiff or fake.
It's a meaningless rule with no real effect.
quiz.explanation: A title acknowledges the difference in the relationship without requiring a stiff or overly formal tone in everything else you say. Most teachers register that small signal of respect even when they never comment on it.

quiz.question: What's the common thread across handshakes, email greetings, and thank-you notes in professional settings?
choices: Small, low-effort signals that show you take the relationship seriously.
Rules that only matter if you get caught breaking them.
quiz.explanation: None of these gestures take much time or effort, but each one signals that you're paying attention to the other person and the relationship. That consistent small effort is what builds a reputation as someone worth working with.

slides.title: Recovering from an awkward moment
slides.text: Everyone occasionally trips, forgets a name, or says the wrong thing in front of people, and the instinct to dwell on it usually makes the moment feel bigger than it actually was to anyone watching. A light acknowledgment — 'Well, that was smooth' — and moving on is called social recovery, and it usually ends the awkwardness faster than ignoring it or over-apologizing.

widgetConfig.scenario: You trip and stumble in front of a group. What's a good way to handle it?

options.label: Laugh it off and keep going
options.outcome: Exactly right! Everyone occasionally trips or says the wrong thing — laughing it off and moving on is a great way to recover.

options.label: Freeze up and refuse to move for the rest of the day
options.outcome: Freezing up makes the moment feel bigger than it is — laughing it off and continuing on works much better.

options.label: Awkward moments can never be recovered from
options.outcome: Awkward moments absolutely can be recovered from — a light laugh and moving on usually does the trick.

slides.title: Small talk has a real purpose
slides.text: Small talk — brief, low-stakes conversation about the weather, a shared class, or someone's weekend — isn't meaningless filler; it's a low-pressure way two people signal they're friendly before anything deeper gets discussed. Asking a genuine follow-up question, not just answering and going quiet, is what keeps small talk from feeling stiff or forced.

widgetConfig.scenario: You think small talk (like "how's the weather") is pointless chit-chat. What's its real value?

options.label: It builds rapport and comfort before deeper conversation
options.outcome: Exactly — small talk isn't really about the weather itself, it's a social tool that builds comfort and connection before more meaningful conversation.

options.label: It has no real purpose at all
options.outcome: Small talk actually serves an important social function — building comfort and rapport before deeper conversations happen.

options.label: It's only for people who have nothing important to say
options.outcome: Even people with plenty to say use small talk — it's a normal way to build initial comfort in a conversation.

slides.title: Manners differ across cultures
slides.text: Manners are not universal. Eye contact, greetings, personal space, volume, and table habits can mean different things across cultures and families. Curiosity and flexibility are more useful than assuming one style is the only polite one.

widgetConfig.scenario: Eye contact and greetings mean different things in different cultures. What's the best mindset?

options.label: Curiosity and flexibility, not assuming one style is the only polite one
options.outcome: Exactly right! Manners are not universal — curiosity and flexibility are more useful than assuming one style is the only polite one.

options.label: Assuming your own culture's manners are the only correct ones
options.outcome: Assuming your own culture's manners are the only correct ones ignores real differences — curiosity and flexibility work much better.

options.label: Manners are identical in every culture
options.outcome: Manners actually vary a lot between cultures — eye contact, greetings, and more can mean different things.

slides.title: Reading the room before you speak
slides.text: A joke that would land perfectly at a casual hangout can fall completely flat, or even seem hurtful, at a solemn event like a funeral or a serious family conversation. Pausing to notice the general mood of a room before speaking, sometimes called situational awareness, prevents a lot of accidental awkwardness before it happens.

widgetConfig.scenario: A joke that works at a casual hangout might not fit a solemn event. What helps?

options.label: Pausing to notice the room's general mood first
options.outcome: Exactly right! Pausing to notice the general mood of a room before speaking prevents a lot of accidental awkwardness.

options.label: Making the same joke no matter the setting
options.outcome: The same joke can land very differently depending on the setting — noticing the mood first helps avoid awkwardness.

options.label: The mood of a room never matters for what you say
options.outcome: The mood of a room actually matters a lot — reading it first helps you avoid a joke falling flat or seeming hurtful.

slides.title: Politely declining without over-explaining
slides.text: A simple 'I appreciate the invite, but I can't make it' is a complete, polite answer on its own, and it doesn't need three extra sentences of justification to be acceptable. Over-explaining a decline can actually invite more questions or pushback than a short, confident no ever would.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend invites you to an event you really don't want to attend. What's the best way to decline?

options.label: Thanks for the invite, but I can't make it this time.
options.outcome: That's a polite, confident decline — a short, warm response is all you need, no lengthy excuse required.

options.label: Give a long, detailed excuse to justify it
options.outcome: Over-explaining can actually sound less believable and makes the moment more awkward than it needs to be.

options.label: Just don't respond to the invite at all
options.outcome: Not responding can come across as rude or make the person worry — a short, polite reply is much kinder.

slides.title: Being present instead of narrating an event
slides.text: Filming or photographing an entire moment — a friend's toast, a sunset, a concert — instead of actually experiencing it can make the people around you feel like an audience for your phone rather than people you're spending time with. Putting the phone down occasionally, even for a memorable moment, is a form of respect for the people actually there.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're at a friend's special moment and keep filming the whole thing on your phone. What does this risk?

options.label: Making people feel like an audience for your phone instead of being with them
options.outcome: Exactly right! Filming an entire moment instead of experiencing it can make people around you feel like an audience for your phone.

options.label: Nothing — filming everything is always fine
options.outcome: Filming everything isn't always fine — it can make the people around you feel less like they're truly being present with you.

options.label: Putting your phone down never matters
options.outcome: Putting your phone down actually matters — it's a form of respect for the people who are actually there with you.

slides.title: Knowing when a joke has gone too far
slides.text: A joke that gets one uncomfortable laugh instead of a real one is usually a signal worth noticing, rather than a cue to push further to get a bigger reaction. Reading that discomfort and shifting topics, instead of doubling down, shows more social skill than any single joke landing well ever could.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your joke gets an uncomfortable laugh instead of a real one. What should you do?

options.label: Notice the discomfort and shift topics
options.outcome: Exactly right! An uncomfortable laugh is usually a signal worth noticing, and shifting topics shows more social skill than pushing further.

options.label: Push further to get a bigger reaction
options.outcome: Pushing further after an uncomfortable laugh usually makes things worse — shifting topics is the better move.

options.label: Uncomfortable laughs always mean the joke worked
options.outcome: An uncomfortable laugh usually signals discomfort, not success — noticing it and shifting topics shows more social skill.

slides.title: Adjusting your tone across different groups
slides.text: Most people naturally adjust their wording, humor, and level of formality depending on the setting. This is often called shifting your communication style; it does not mean changing your values or pretending to be someone else.

widgetConfig.scenario: You naturally talk differently with close friends than with a teacher. Does this mean you're being fake?

options.label: No — adjusting tone to the setting is normal, not fake
options.outcome: Exactly right! Most people naturally adjust their wording, humor, and formality depending on the setting — this isn't being fake.

options.label: Yes, you should talk exactly the same way everywhere
options.outcome: Talking exactly the same way everywhere ignores that different settings call for different tones — adjusting is completely normal.

options.label: Adjusting your tone means pretending to be someone else
options.outcome: Adjusting your tone doesn't mean pretending to be someone else — it just means shifting your communication style, not your values.

quiz.question: You trip in the hallway in front of your class. What tends to end the awkwardness fastest?
choices: Dwelling on it and apologizing repeatedly.
A light acknowledgment, then moving on.
quiz.explanation: Social recovery — a brief, light acknowledgment like 'that was smooth' — usually ends an awkward moment faster than ignoring it or over-apologizing. Dwelling on it tends to make the moment feel bigger to everyone watching than it actually was.

quiz.question: A classmate asks how your weekend was, and you answer in one word without asking anything back. What's missing?
choices: A genuine follow-up question to keep it going.
Nothing — small talk is meaningless anyway.
quiz.explanation: Small talk is a low-pressure way two people signal they're friendly before anything deeper comes up. A genuine follow-up question is what keeps it feeling natural instead of stiff or like an interrogation.

quiz.question: You're surprised that a foreign exchange student avoids direct eye contact with adults. What's the more gracious response?
choices: Assume they're being rude or dishonest.
Recognize it may reflect a different cultural norm.
quiz.explanation: Eye contact norms vary a lot across cultures, and what reads as respectful in one place can read as aggressive in another. Cultural humility means considering that difference before assuming your own family's norm is the only correct one.

quiz.question: You're at a solemn family gathering and start to make a joke you'd normally make with friends. What should you do?
choices: Read the room and hold off on the joke.
Tell it anyway since it's usually funny.
quiz.explanation: Situational awareness means noticing a room's general mood before speaking, since a joke that lands at a casual hangout can seem hurtful at a solemn event. Pausing to read the room first prevents a lot of accidental awkwardness.

quiz.question: You're invited somewhere you don't want to go. What's a complete, polite way to decline?
choices: A short 'I appreciate the invite, but I can't make it.'
A long list of excuses to justify saying no.
quiz.explanation: A brief, confident decline is a complete answer on its own and doesn't require extra justification to be acceptable. Over-explaining can actually invite more questions or pushback than a short, polite no would.

quiz.question: You spend a friend's entire birthday toast filming it instead of watching. What might that communicate?
choices: Nothing — filming shows you care about the memory.
That your phone matters more than the moment itself.
quiz.explanation: Filming an entire moment instead of experiencing it can make people around you feel like an audience for your phone rather than people you're actually with. Putting the phone down occasionally is a form of respect for the people there.

quiz.question: You tell a joke and get one uncomfortable, forced laugh instead of a real one. What's the better move?
choices: Push further to try to land a bigger laugh.
Notice the discomfort and shift topics.
quiz.explanation: A forced or uncomfortable laugh is usually a signal worth noticing rather than a cue to escalate the joke further. Reading that discomfort and changing the subject shows more social skill than any single joke landing well.

quiz.question: You're more relaxed and joking with close friends than you are at a formal family dinner. Is that being fake?
choices: Yes, you should act exactly the same everywhere.
No — adjusting tone to the room is normal.
quiz.explanation: This natural shifting between contexts, called adjusting your communication style, is something almost everyone does instinctively rather than a form of dishonesty. Both versions are genuinely you, just adjusted for who's actually in the room with you.

quiz.question: Why does small talk matter even though the topics themselves — weather, weekends — feel trivial?
choices: It's a low-pressure way people signal friendliness before deeper conversation.
It has no real function and can be skipped entirely.
quiz.explanation: The specific topic of small talk usually isn't the point — it's a low-stakes way for two people to establish that they're friendly. Skipping straight past it can actually make a deeper conversation feel more abrupt.

quiz.question: What connects reading the room before a joke and noticing an uncomfortable laugh mid-joke?
choices: Both involve paying attention to how others are actually reacting.
Both mean you should never tell jokes around others.
quiz.explanation: Situational awareness before speaking and noticing discomfort while speaking are really the same skill applied at different moments. Both rely on paying attention to the people around you instead of only your own intentions.

slides.title: Being a good host, not just a guest
slides.text: A good host checks in during the event — 'Do you need anything? Have you met everyone?' — instead of only greeting people at the door and then disappearing into their own conversation. Hosting well means periodically noticing who looks unsure or left out and quietly including them, which is a form of attentiveness rather than a rigid script to follow.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're hosting a get-together. What makes you a good host beyond just greeting people at the door?

options.label: Checking in during the event and including people who look left out
options.outcome: Exactly right! Hosting well means periodically noticing who looks unsure or left out and quietly including them.

options.label: Greeting people, then disappearing into your own conversation
options.outcome: Greeting people and then disappearing misses the ongoing attentiveness that makes someone a genuinely good host.

options.label: Hosting well only means decorating nicely
options.outcome: Decorating nicely is nice, but hosting well is really about checking in on your guests throughout the event.

slides.title: Formal meal etiquette, one piece at a time
slides.text: At a formal meal, the general rule for silverware is to work from the outside in, using the outermost fork or spoon first for each course as it arrives. You don't need to memorize every utensil in advance; watching your host and starting from the outside gets you through almost any formal table setting.

widgetConfig.scenario: At a formal dinner, there are multiple forks and spoons at your place setting. Which one should you use first?

options.label: The outermost utensil, working inward with each course
options.outcome: Exactly! The general rule is to work from the outside in as each course arrives.

options.label: Whichever utensil looks biggest
options.outcome: Size isn't the rule — working from the outermost utensil inward with each course is the standard etiquette.

options.label: It doesn't matter which one you use
options.outcome: It does matter at a formal meal — the outside-in order is the expected etiquette.

slides.title: Hosting invitations with useful details
slides.text: A good invitation answers the questions a guest will actually have — time, location, what to bring, how long it's expected to last — instead of leaving them to guess and ask around. Thinking through those details ahead of time is a quiet form of hospitality that guests notice even if they never mention it.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're inviting friends to an event. What makes a good invitation?

options.label: Including time, location, what to bring, and how long it'll last
options.outcome: Exactly right! A good invitation answers the questions a guest will actually have, instead of leaving them to guess.

options.label: Leaving guests to guess all the details
options.outcome: Leaving guests to guess the details makes planning harder for them — including useful details is more thoughtful.

options.label: Details in an invitation never matter
options.outcome: Details in an invitation actually matter a lot — guests notice when you've thought it through, even if they never mention it.

slides.title: Cultural differences at someone else's table
slides.text: A meal eaten with hands instead of utensils, or a greeting that involves a bow instead of a handshake, isn't a lesser version of 'normal' — it's simply a different tradition with its own logic and history. Approaching an unfamiliar custom with curiosity instead of visible surprise is a quiet but noticeable form of respect.

widgetConfig.scenario: A meal is eaten with hands instead of utensils, which is unfamiliar to you. What's the respectful response?

options.label: Approach it with curiosity instead of visible surprise
options.outcome: Exactly right! Approaching an unfamiliar custom with curiosity instead of visible surprise is a quiet but noticeable form of respect.

options.label: React with obvious surprise or judgment
options.outcome: Reacting with obvious surprise can feel disrespectful — curiosity shows much more respect for a different tradition.

options.label: Assume it's a lesser way of doing things
options.outcome: An unfamiliar custom isn't a lesser version of normal — it's simply a different tradition with its own logic and history.

slides.title: Handling a compliment or criticism gracefully
slides.text: A simple "thank you" is enough when someone gives you a compliment. With criticism, listen for anything useful, ask questions if needed, and remember that you can disagree respectfully with feedback that feels unfair or inaccurate.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone gives you constructive criticism about a project you worked hard on. What's the most graceful response?

options.label: Thank them for the feedback, even if it stings a little
options.outcome: That's graceful handling — accepting feedback with appreciation (even when it's hard to hear) shows maturity and helps you actually improve.

options.label: Get defensive and argue that they're wrong
options.outcome: Getting defensive can shut down useful feedback and make people hesitant to be honest with you in the future.

options.label: Pretend you don't care at all
options.outcome: Dismissing it entirely means missing a chance to actually learn from it — graceful acceptance, even briefly, works better.

slides.title: Punctuality as a form of respect
slides.text: Being on time helps other people plan and shows reliability. Delays happen, so the respectful move is to communicate when you can rather than assuming lateness automatically means someone does not care.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're running 20 minutes late to meet a friend, with no real reason. What does this communicate?

options.label: It can feel like their time wasn't valued as much as yours
options.outcome: Exactly — consistent lateness, even unintentional, can unintentionally signal that someone's time matters less to you. Punctuality is a simple way to show respect.

options.label: It doesn't communicate anything at all
options.outcome: Being late, especially repeatedly, often does send an unintended message about how much you value the other person's time.

options.label: It shows you're very busy and important
options.outcome: Lateness is more likely to feel disrespectful than impressive — punctuality is generally seen as a sign of respect.

slides.title: Navigating a business or formal dinner
slides.text: At a formal or professional meal, follow the host's cues, choose something you can eat comfortably, and focus on conversation and courtesy. Traditions about who starts eating or what to order vary by setting and culture.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're at a formal professional dinner and unsure of the customs. What should you do?

options.label: Follow the host's cues and focus on conversation and courtesy
options.outcome: Exactly right! At a formal or professional meal, following the host's cues and focusing on conversation and courtesy works well.

options.label: Ignore the host's lead and do your own thing
options.outcome: Ignoring the host's lead can feel out of step with the occasion — following their cues is a better approach.

options.label: Formal dinner customs are identical everywhere
options.outcome: Formal dinner customs actually vary by setting and culture — following the host's lead helps you navigate them.

slides.title: Gracious gift-giving and gift-receiving
slides.text: A thoughtful gift doesn't need to be expensive — it needs to show you paid attention to the person, which is what actually makes it feel personal rather than generic. On the receiving end, reacting with genuine warmth rather than immediately commenting on cost or usefulness respects the thought the giver put into choosing it.

widgetConfig.scenario: You receive a gift that isn't expensive. What makes it feel personal anyway?

options.label: That the giver paid attention to who you are
options.outcome: Exactly right! A thoughtful gift doesn't need to be expensive — it needs to show the giver paid attention to who you are.

options.label: Only the price of the gift matters
options.outcome: Price isn't really what makes a gift feel personal — thoughtful attention to who you are matters much more.

options.label: Commenting on the cost is the polite response
options.outcome: Commenting on the cost can feel dismissive — reacting with genuine warmth respects the thought the giver put into it.

quiz.question: You're hosting a party and greet everyone at the door, then spend the rest of the night with your closest friends. What's missing?
choices: Nothing — greeting guests at the door is enough.
Periodically checking in on guests throughout the event.
quiz.explanation: Good hosting means noticing who looks unsure or left out during the event, not just at the door. A quick 'Have you met everyone?' partway through shows attentiveness that a greeting alone doesn't cover.

quiz.question: You're at a formal dinner with multiple forks at your place setting. What's a simple rule to follow?
choices: Use the outermost utensil first, working inward with each course.
Guess randomly since it doesn't actually matter.
quiz.explanation: The general rule for formal place settings is to work from the outside in, using the outermost fork or spoon first. Combined with watching your host, that one rule gets you through almost any formal table.

quiz.question: You're sending a party invitation. What makes it genuinely useful to your guests?
choices: Including time, location, and what to bring.
Keeping it vague so people can ask questions later.
quiz.explanation: A good invitation answers the practical questions a guest will actually have, instead of leaving them to guess or track you down. Thinking through those details ahead of time is a quiet, noticeable form of hospitality.

quiz.question: A friend's family eats a meal with their hands instead of utensils, which surprises you. What's the more gracious response?
choices: React with visible surprise or discomfort.
Approach the custom with curiosity, not surprise.
quiz.explanation: A different eating custom isn't a lesser version of 'normal' — it's a different tradition with its own logic and history. Meeting it with curiosity instead of visible surprise is a quiet but real form of respect.

quiz.question: Someone compliments your project. What's a better response than 'oh, it was nothing'?
choices: 'Thank you, that means a lot.'
'oh, it was nothing.'
quiz.explanation: Deflecting a genuine compliment can make the other person feel like their kind words weren't actually welcome. A simple, direct 'thank you' accepts the compliment gracefully without brushing it aside.

quiz.question: Why is punctuality useful when other people are depending on you?
choices: It helps people plan and shows reliability.
Being on time never affects anyone else.
quiz.explanation: Being on time helps other people plan. If a delay happens, communicating about it is usually more respectful than disappearing without an update.

quiz.question: At a formal dinner and unsure when to start eating, what's a good approach?
choices: Start immediately without noticing anyone else.
Follow the host's cues or wait until the group begins.
quiz.explanation: Formal meal customs vary, so watching the host or group is a practical way to handle an unfamiliar setting.

quiz.question: You receive a gift and immediately ask how much it cost. What does that overlook?
choices: That the gift's value was in the thought, not the price.
That gifts should always be returned if inexpensive.
quiz.explanation: A thoughtful gift doesn't need to be expensive to feel personal — what matters is that it shows attention to the receiver. Reacting with genuine warmth instead of commenting on cost respects the thought behind it.

quiz.question: A friend gives you fair, calm criticism about something you did. What shows more maturity?
choices: Accepting it without getting visibly defensive.
Arguing every point they make.
quiz.explanation: Accepting fair criticism gracefully, the same way you'd accept a genuine compliment, shows real maturity in how you handle feedback. Getting visibly defensive tends to shut down a conversation that could actually be useful to you.

quiz.question: What's the common thread between good hosting, punctuality, and gracious gift-receiving?
choices: Each one shows attentiveness to other people's time or effort.
Each one requires spending a lot of money.
quiz.explanation: Checking in on guests, showing up on time, and appreciating a thoughtful gift all come down to noticing and valuing what someone else put into the moment. None of them require money — just attention.
